narrator.instruct: Fast-paced, energetic, punchy explainer narrator. Brisk delivery with no long pauses.

firefighter.instruct: Calm, dry, slightly amused firefighter. Short and confident.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You've hit the close door button six times, and the doors haven't moved.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You're late for a job interview on floor forty.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A firefighter strolls toward the lobby. You jab the button even harder.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The doors finally slide shut. You're sure your thumb did that.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Floor twelve. The doors open, and the firefighter steps in.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: She turns a key, taps the same button, and the doors slam shut instantly.

lines.speaker: firefighter
lines.text: Oh, it works. Just not for you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: In nineteen ninety, America passed a big disability law.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Elevator doors must stay open long enough for wheelchairs and crutches.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That's at least three seconds, and your button can't cut it short.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So in many elevators, it's wired to basically nothing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It only wakes up in fire mode, when firefighters need full control.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And crosswalks lie too. In two thousand four, New York checked its walk buttons.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Of three thousand two hundred fifty, over two thousand five hundred did nothing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: They were leftovers from the nineteen seventies, before computers ran the lights.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ripping them out would cost a million dollars, so the city just left them.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You reach floor forty, two minutes late.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And down in the lobby, someone new is hitting that button.
